answer_md:

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. In teams he inherited, engineers were often “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, some teams avoided risks because they feared blame. Matt pushed decisions to the people closest to the work, made intent explicit, and used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. For engineers facing cloud-native knowledge gaps, he paired senior and junior team members, introduced weekly peer-led demos, and embedded learning in live client projects.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. The balanced-team work reduced project delays, improved team satisfaction and retention, and achieved **zero-defect production code**. Mentorship also reduced onboarding time for new hires.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 On it!

At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt’s balanced-team model and emphasis on test-driven development did not prevent a quality crisis. In early **2020**, the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement was modernizing the client’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, as the pandemic forced remote work, the client reported rising defects despite dashboards showing near-complete test coverage. The concerns landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

An engineer had been building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete while defects went undetected. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done. Introducing the team structure and practices had not established how people actually worked.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly, including problems in the backlog. He brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team and redo the code and tests.

He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and introduced boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and an “I do, we do, you do” coaching progression. He also restructured agile ceremonies to keep stakeholders, developers, and product managers working from the same requirements.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Client and account-leadership confidence returned through the open audit and visible improvement.

answer_md:
🐾 Yes. In one engagement, Matt took accountability, but the team member involved still bore an individual consequence.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases.

Matt’s responsibility was to ensure a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on inherited documentation without confirming its accuracy. He did not audit who could trigger downstream email processes, verify that production customer data had been scrubbed, or implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. But the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

That is a limit to the “permit to fail” environment described earlier: in this incident, taking accountability did not prevent the tester’s removal. It was also a failure in Matt’s own responsibilities before the incident, not just a problem with the client’s response.

Matt’s stated change afterward was to treat IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership as day-one leadership responsibilities, rather than assuming inherited controls were correct.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Tracking this down...

At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt’s initial rollout of balanced teams, pairing, and test-driven development did not prevent a quality crisis. A couple of months into the Revenue and Shipment Planning modernization, the client reported rising defects while the team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, just as the pandemic moved work remote.

Pairing, test-first, and continuous integration had been in place from the start, but the reinforcement and verification had been missing. An engineer was building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done. Coverage looked complete while defects went undetected.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership instead of defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite, exposed the gaps, and rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. He brought in frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team and redo the code and tests properly.

The follow-up changed the daily workflow, not just the training: test cases became a discrete step before engineering the solution, checked at stand-up. New engineers paired with seasoned practitioners, pairs rotated daily, and stories were capped at **3** points within **1-week** iterations.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Pairing and test-first remained the default after the experts left, and the crisis failure mode did not recur. Matt’s stated lesson was that “implementing a practice is the easy half,” with reinforcement, follow-up, and verification needed to make it real.

question: Would he relocate?

answer_md:
🐾 On it!

On a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client, Matt assumed the inherited access controls and environment boundaries were correct. He was the tech lead, responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but relied on existing documentation rather than verifying the configuration. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production.

That assumption led to an actual incident: an offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT that sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands** of real clients.

Matt had not audited who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes. He had not verified whether customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments, or implemented compensating controls such as data masking and email interception. He had focused on delivery pressures instead of validating those access patterns.

After the incident, Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The investigation identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His stated lesson was that leaders own the environment their teams operate in. He made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

He used a Client Onboarding Test Drive to gather end-user feedback and integrated CI/CD updates for documentation and APIs.

answer_md:
🐾 Perfect, here's what I found.

At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt faced a quality crisis during the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement in **2020**. Pairing also faced explicit resistance: “I’m not paying for **two** people to do the work of **one**.” Matt let skeptics experience it firsthand. A **2-day** CIC Academy course, delivered **twice monthly** over **6 months**, accompanied contributors pairing into the new-state build.

The MVP covered **95%** of targeted use cases. EDI validation notified trading partners proactively, the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and client contributors gained the skills to support the application after **Accenture** rolled off.

question: How long did that take?

answer_md:
🐾 Here's a great example.

At **Accenture**, Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers as client demand grew, but many new hires lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience. The documented starting point was a **10-person pilot**, rather than **4**. Over **4 years**, the centers grew to **150+ practitioners** across engineering, architecture, product, and design, not engineering alone.

Matt built a hiring engine across internal bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions rather than relying on interview discussion alone. Interviewers recorded independent votes, and Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process handled **15 to 20 auditions per week**, producing **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**. Interview participation was capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** to protect delivery time.

He recruited for learning potential and collaborative mindsets, then used tailored enablement, experienced mentors, and rotating pair partners. Practitioners progressed through “I do, we do, you do” toward independent delivery. Weekly peer-led demonstrations, skills matrices, and career development conversations continued after onboarding. Recruiting, hackathons, and job fairs at Georgia Tech also expanded the talent pipeline.

Matt kept the organization deliberately flat: **11 to 13 practice and client leads** reported directly to him through a **2-layer structure**. Team anchors kept leads informed without adding middle management. Monday allocation reviews matched practitioners to engagements and learning work, while evaluations drew on evidence from recent pair partners rather than a manager’s impressions.

The organization reached **150+ practitioners** with near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**. Across the centers, **10-person balanced teams** delivered equivalent output to traditional **20-person teams**, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments. Delivery excellence and client referrals helped generate **\$100M+ in repeatable business** by **FY23**.

A Client Onboarding Test Drive gathered end-user feedback.

answer_md:
🐾 Found it! Matt was brought in roughly seven months into **Fiserv**'s 14-month, **$8.5M** white-label card portal program, the shared platform behind branded credit card sites for **2M+** cardholders across **15** financial institutions. The **45-person** globally dispersed team had missed multiple consecutive deadlines, and client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. He recovered a Q4 release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **$500K** in penalties, and the program was delivered **3%** under budget with zero critical defects at launch.

Want to hear how he moved that team from 6-month waterfall releases to 2-week sprints?

🐾 Found it!

At **Fiserv**, the **45-person** team was working through **6-month** waterfall release cycles without visibility into work status. Requirements lived in a **200-page** business requirements document organized by system modules. Developers in India, testers in the Philippines, and designers in Ireland were working across time zones while deadlines slipped. PMO and compliance resisted agile, and some stakeholders lacked bandwidth for feedback every **2 weeks**.

Matt changed how the team defined and tracked work. He decomposed the requirements into persona-based user stories and replaced a single To Do/Done JIRA board with a multi-tiered Kanban/Scrum structure. The **47** acceptance criteria became Epics, with user stories moving through specific workflow columns. Offshore-to-onshore handoffs happened at **7 AM CST**, with reverse handoffs at **11 PM CST**.

Instead of waiting until month **6** to discover branding, UI, or accessibility problems, Matt introduced demos every **2 weeks**. He negotiated dedicated review windows so decisions would not stall sprint work. He maintained steering committee reporting while adding sprint-level visibility.

For compliance reviewers, JIRA held audit trails, attached ADA scans, and developer comments rather than relying on static Word documents. Matt coached offshore teams on empowerment over command-and-control and built JAWS/NVDA screen reader audits into the Definition of Done. Accessibility training also meant developers could maintain compliance on subsequent releases without external accessibility expertise.

Within **3 months**, the team had moved to **2-week** sprints. More than **50** stakeholders across **3** time zones gained real-time work visibility, and PMO and compliance accepted JIRA as the system of record. Separately, build-pipeline changes eliminated SVN merge conflicts that had blocked engineers, reduced builds from days to hours, and replaced frequent hotfixes and WAR rollbacks with predictable, quality-controlled releases.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s work at **Norfolk Southern**.

As a Director at **Accenture**, Matt led Revenue and Shipment Planning modernization from **November 2019** through **September 2023**, the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement. The railroad’s mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. The client organization worked around mainframe practices, account leadership expected waterfall delivery, and Matt’s team was learning new ways of working as the pandemic forced remote work.

Matt brought cross-workstream representatives together for domain-driven design and event storming to map business functions, data flows, and dependencies. Using the Boris Exercise and SNAP-E documentation, the team defined APIs, boundaries, and integration risks. The mainframe remained the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB rose beside it, connected through change data capture and reconciliation.

When client stakeholders grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System interface through personas, prototypes, and weekly build-measure-learn iterations.

The engagement also hit a quality crisis: defects rose despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership, audited the code and tests, and exposed vague backlog stories and tests written after code. He brought in TDD experts, rebuilt testable stories, and reinforced test-first work through rotating pairs, coding katas, and coaching.

Alongside delivery, Matt led a **2-day** CIC Academy course delivered twice monthly over **6 months**. Pairing spread scarce domain knowledge and helped client contributors learn Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native concepts.

The MVP launched covering **95%** of targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation detected fallout proactively rather than waiting for customer calls. The work scaled to **3 balanced teams**, and client contributors gained the skills to support and manage the new application.

question: Tell me about his Norfolk Southern work.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what Matt worked on at **RBC**.

From **June 2012** to **June 2013**, Matt served as Senior Technology Architecture Manager on **RBC’s** Day**2Day** Corporate Banking modernization. The bank’s existing systems had performance and scalability limitations and lacked digital offerings. **RBC** was evaluating Bottomline WebSeries as the payment hub engine to replace its aging **RBC** Express portal, and leadership needed to know whether the platform could meet its requirements before committing further investment.

Matt conducted an architecture assessment and gap/fit analysis, using code reviews, stakeholder interviews, documentation analysis, and architectural heat maps. He assessed Data, Application, Technology, and Business Architecture and worked with the bank’s enterprise architecture team on target-system models and a cost-to-fix versus benefit comparison. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the modularity required for **RBC’s** long-term digital operating model. That finding prevented investment in a platform path that could not deliver and enabled the bank to redirect technical resources toward higher-priority initiatives.

Alongside that assessment, Matt established the PMO. He developed the project management plan, maintained the program roadmap and dependencies, and coordinated reporting across **RBC**, **Accenture**, and Bottomline Technologies. Designated team contacts, daily summaries, and a task-tracking matrix eliminated missed program updates, reduced redundant efforts, and clarified resource assignments.

When the previous data conversion lead left early in the initiative, Matt took over the workstream from scratch. He analyzed legacy payment records, documented source-to-target transformation rules, planned mock conversion cycles, and established reconciliation checks for payment amounts and beneficiary details. He delivered an end-to-end conversion plan and coordinated onshore and offshore data-scrubbing and validation teams.

He also assessed mobile readiness, defining API integration points, cheque deposit requirements, and cross-device scalability needs. The resulting modernization blueprint covered mobile capabilities and real-time account access. The reported outcomes were the investment decision, governance framework, conversion plan, and mobile blueprint, rather than a quantified savings figure or completed platform launch.
